title: Write cells and save
summary: Give a cell a value with ws["D1"] = "Total" or ws.cell(row=r, column=c, value=v), then wb.save("new.xlsx"). Formulas are written as text starting with =; Excel works them out when the file is opened.
objectives: Write values into cells by address and by number.
Add a new column worked out row by row.
Write an Excel formula into a cell, and know it isn’t calculated by Python.
Save the workbook, under a new name so the original is safe.

slides.h: By the end: a Value column, added for you
slides.say: Meera adds a Value column to the stock sheet every week by hand. By the end of this lesson Python adds it, fills every row and saves a new file.
points: Writing a cell looks like setting a variable: `ws["D1"] = "Value"`.
Nothing is saved until you call `wb.save(...)`.
p: Meera adds a Value column to the stock sheet every week by hand. By the end of this lesson Python adds it, fills every row and saves a new file.
Writing a cell looks like setting a variable: `ws["D1"] = "Value"`.
Nothing is saved until you call `wb.save(...)`.

visual.text:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
ws["D1"] = "Value"
for r in range(2, ws.max_row + 1):
    ws.cell(row=r, column=4).value = ws.cell(row=r, column=2).value * ws.cell(row=r, column=3).value
wb.save("stock_value.xlsx")
print("Saved")
notes: A header for the new column
D = B × C on every row

slides.h: Two ways to write a cell
slides.say: By address when you know it, by number inside a loop.
points: `ws.cell(row=r, column=4, value=99)` does the same in one call.
p: By address when you know it, by number inside a loop.
`ws.cell(row=r, column=4, value=99)` does the same in one call.

bad.title: Easy to get wrong in a loop

slides.say: `wb.save("stock.xlsx")` replaces the original file, with no undo. While you are learning, save to a new name and open both to compare.
points: A new name keeps the original safe.
If the file is open in Excel, saving over it fails with PermissionError.

visual.text: Habit worth keeping: read from `stock.xlsx`, save to `stock_report.xlsx`. If anything is wrong, the original is untouched.

check.q: You set `ws["E1"] = "Notes"` and the program ends. What is in the file?
options: Nothing has changed: there was no wb.save()
check.explain: Changes live in memory until you save.

slides.say: A text that starts with `=` is stored as a formula, exactly as if you’d typed it in Excel. Excel calculates it when someone opens the file.
points: The formula updates in Excel if someone changes a number.
p: A text that starts with `=` is stored as a formula, exactly as if you’d typed it in Excel. Excel calculates it when someone opens the file.
The formula updates in Excel if someone changes a number.

visual.text:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
ws["D1"] = "Value"
for r in range(2, ws.max_row + 1):
    ws.cell(row=r, column=4, value=f"=B{r}*C{r}")
wb.save("stock_formulas.xlsx")

slides.say: openpyxl writes the formula but doesn’t work it out. Reading that cell back in Python gives the formula text, not a number.
points: Need the number in Python? Calculate it in Python and write the value.
Need a live formula for the person using Excel? Write the formula.

  File "main.py", line 5, in <module>
    print(ws["D2"].value + 1)
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
visual.right:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
ws["D2"] = ws["B2"].value * ws["C2"].value
print(ws["D2"].value + 1)

check.explain: Python stores the formula as text; Excel works it out later.

demo.intro: Watch a Value column added to the stock sheet and saved as a new file.

steps.type:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
ws["D1"] = "Value"
for r in range(2, ws.max_row):
    qty = ws.cell(row=r, column=2).value
    price = ws.cell(row=r, column=3).value
    ws.cell(row=r, column=4, value=qty * price)
wb.save("stock_value.xlsx")

steps.say: Look at the new file: the last row, Files, has no value. range stops one early: it needs max_row + 1.
Every row has its value now, and stock.xlsx itself is unchanged.

demo.outro: Your turn: write cells and save.
demo.final:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
ws["D1"] = "Value"
for r in range(2, ws.max_row + 1):
    qty = ws.cell(row=r, column=2).value
    price = ws.cell(row=r, column=3).value
    ws.cell(row=r, column=4, value=qty * price)
wb.save("stock_value.xlsx")

tasks.model:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
ws["D1"] = "Value"
last = ws.max_row
for r in range(2, last + 1):
    ws.cell(row=r, column=4, value=f"=B{r}*C{r}")
ws.cell(row=last + 1, column=4, value=f"=SUM(D2:D{last})")
wb.save("stock_value.xlsx")
tasks.explain: f"=B{r}*C{r}" builds each formula; the SUM goes on the row after the last.
hints: An f-string can build the formula text.
Remember the last row before you add the SUM row.

practice.prompt: Write **Reorder** in column D for every item with fewer than 50 left (leave the others empty), and save **stock_reorder.xlsx**.
practice.model:
import openpyxl
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook("stock.xlsx")
ws = wb["Stock"]
for r in range(2, ws.max_row + 1):
    if ws.cell(row=r, column=2).value < 50:
        ws.cell(row=r, column=4, value="Reorder")
wb.save("stock_reorder.xlsx")
